question: What is the meaning of manufacturing process and techniques in relation to object characteristics (objective registered data related to circularity)?
data_group: object characteristics (objective registered data related to circularity)
description: The manufacturing process and techniques are crucial in determining the object characteristics, which are registered data related to circularity. These characteristics include material passport, physical properties, and other facets of the MPO, which are used to describe the product, component, and material combinations and their properties. The registered data related to circularity, such as sustainability and recyclability, are influenced by the manufacturing process and techniques, which can affect the material passport, physical properties, and other facets of the MPO. Therefore, understanding the manufacturing process and techniques is essential for accurately registering data related to circularity.

references.text:
3.1
Ontology facets
The MPO has material passport, physical property, composite material, sustainability
property, temporal property, thermal property, and chemical and biological property facets.
The role of each facet is described in the sections that follow.
3.1.1
Material passport
Figure 3 shows the material passport facet. This is the core of the MPO. It defines a
Material Passport that describes combinations of Product, Component, and Material to
ensure that sufficient information is available to support circularity considerations.
Product, Component, and Material can have a Manufacturer described by various datatype
properties. They have a hasProperty relation to Property that allows the specification
of Physical, Composition, Temporal, Thermal, Sustainability, Chemical, and Biological
properties via the other facets. These enable identification and traversal to further detail.
Figure 3: Material passport facet of the MPO.
Product and Component have datatype properties (e.g., id, name, description, hasGTIN,
and hasEAN) to store additional metadata. For example, a chassis is a product used in
the manufacture of automotive vehicles. A chassis hasPart crossbeam, which has a ma-
terial passport that includes descriptors like name, description, European Article Number
(EAN), Global Trade Item Number (GTIN), etc. alongside details of the manufacturer.
3.1.2
Physical properties
Figure 4 shows the physical property facet. This is used to describe characteristics like
density, mass, and rigidity. These are important because they facilitate the calculation
of the MCI, enabling the identification of recoverable, reusable and recyclable parts of
products, thereby promoting the principles of circularity.

environmental life cycle registrations but concern all types of life cycle

of larger objects (e.g., a house) by means of replacement, circulation, 
etc., life cycle data may reside at the small object level, and may be 
governed externally, but can be linked for use in the larger object. 
Therefore, we must interpret passports as an interface to multiple 
components and possibly the lower-level hierarchical components of 
these, which each are in turn concerned with an individual life cycle 
history. 
7. Passports have the ultimate goal to yield insight into the 
sustainability and circularity characteristics, the circular value 
estimation, and the circular opportunities. These are basically a 
reformulation of the top 3 goals revealed by this study (see Section 3.8). 
Firstly, it helps to understand the sustainability and circularity of a 
product, for example, in determining which product to acquire or 
whether a product should be replaced. Secondly, it supports in identi­
fying and estimating the value of components susceptible for circular 
use. Thirdly, it lists the alternative circular options and provides advise
